opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core intuition is actually pretty simple. Take a task like multi-digit addition, and suppose you're scoring it with exact match: the model only gets credit if every single output token is correct. Now imagine that the model's per-token accuracy, the probability it gets any individual digit right, is improving smoothly and predictably as you scale up parameters or compute. That's roughly what we see when we look at things like cross-entropy loss, which tends to follow nice power-law trends.

But if you need, say, L tokens all correct, then your probability of an exact match is roughly that per-token probability raised to the power L. And when you take a quantity that's improving smoothly and raise it to a large power, you get this very characteristic shape. For a long time the result sits near zero, because even 80 or 90 percent per-token accuracy to the tenth power is small. Then as per-token accuracy approaches one, the exact-match score shoots up quite rapidly, and then it saturates. So you get that S-shaped, sharp-looking curve, which people read as the model suddenly acquiring an ability.

Our point was that much of that sharpness comes from the metric, not necessarily from some discontinuous change inside the model. The underlying competence is changing gradually; it's the nonlinear, all-or-nothing scoring that makes it look abrupt. You can test this in a couple of ways. One is to switch to a continuous metric, like token edit distance, or per-token accuracy itself, and when you do that for the same models and the same outputs, the curves often become smooth and predictable. Another is to go the other direction and show you can manufacture emergence: pick a task where performance is smoothly improving, apply a harsh threshold metric, and suddenly you see the same jumpy curve.

There's also a resolution piece. If your test set is small, you can't estimate very small probabilities, so everything below some threshold just reads as zero. That flat region at the start of the S-curve is partly a measurement artifact too. With enough samples you can often see the performance creeping up well before the supposed jump.

I'd add one caveat, because people sometimes overread the conclusion. We're not saying models never undergo interesting qualitative changes, or that nothing surprising happens with scale. The claim is narrower: a lot of the specific evidence for emergent abilities, especially on these arithmetic-style benchmarks, is well explained by the researcher's choice of metric interacting with smooth underlying improvement. And practically, that's good news, because it means if you pick your measurements carefully you can often forecast these capabilities rather than being caught off guard by them.

r001.rationale: It explains that exact-match success requires every token to be correct, so whole-answer accuracy is approximately the per-token accuracy raised to the number of tokens, producing a sharp S-shaped rise as token accuracy improves.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the setup is pretty simple. Take a multi-digit arithmetic problem, say adding two four-digit numbers, and ask what the model has to get right to be marked correct under exact-match accuracy. It has to produce every single output token correctly. If the answer is five digits long, that's five tokens in a row with no mistakes.

Now suppose the model's per-token accuracy is some probability p. As you scale the model, p improves smoothly, roughly in line with the smooth improvements in cross-entropy loss that everyone already agrees are predictable. But the metric we're looking at isn't p, it's p raised to the power of the number of tokens, because you need all of them right. So if p goes from 0.5 to 0.9, that looks like a nice gradual improvement at the per-token level. But p to the fifth goes from about 3 percent to about 59 percent. That's your sharp jump.

That's really the whole story of the S-shape. When p is low, p to the L is essentially zero across a wide range of model sizes, so the curve is flat along the bottom. Then once p crosses some threshold, the exponentiated quantity shoots up very quickly, and then it saturates near one as p approaches one. You get the flat, then the steep part, then the plateau, and it looks for all the world like an ability that switched on at some critical scale. But nothing discontinuous happened to the model. The nonlinearity is entirely in how the metric compounds per-token performance.

And the nice thing is this gives you a prediction you can check. If this story is right, the apparent sharpness should depend on the target length. Longer answers, more tokens that all have to be correct, a sharper and later-looking transition. Shorter answers, a gentler curve. And that's roughly what you see. The other prediction is that if you swap out exact-match for something that gives partial credit, like token-edit distance, which rewards getting most of the digits right, the cliff should disappear and you should see the same smooth, predictable improvement you see in loss. And in our experiments on the GPT-3 family, that's exactly what happened. Same models, same outputs, same task. Change the metric and emergence goes away.

So I'd frame it this way. The toy model isn't claiming the models don't get better at arithmetic. They clearly do. It's saying that the specific shape people pointed to as evidence of something qualitatively new, that sudden jump, is what you'd expect from a smooth underlying process observed through a metric that's discontinuous or very nonlinear in the thing that's actually improving. The researcher's choice of metric creates the S-curve, not the model.

r001.rationale: The response explains that exact-match success requires every output token to be correct, making whole-answer accuracy p^L; as per-token accuracy rises smoothly, this can create a flat-then-steep S-shaped curve.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that getting an arithmetic problem right requires getting several pieces right together. Suppose, in a very simple model, the probability of getting each piece right is p, and there are k pieces. If we assume they’re independent, the probability of getting the entire answer right is p to the k.

Now imagine that p improves smoothly as the model gets better. When p is low, the probability of getting all those pieces right is tiny, so your measured accuracy looks essentially flat. As p gets higher, you start getting complete answers right much more frequently, and then eventually you saturate near perfect accuracy. That can give you this S-shaped curve that looks like a capability suddenly emerged, even though the underlying improvement was gradual.

The point isn’t that arithmetic really consists of independent steps—that’s a simplifying assumption. It’s that the way we combine those steps and score the final answer can produce a sharp-looking transition. So the curve alone doesn’t establish that something discontinuous happened inside the model.

r001.rationale: It models a complete answer as requiring all k independent pieces to be correct, with probability p^k, and explains how rising p yields an S-shaped curve in whole-answer accuracy. “Pieces” conveys the required components of the answer.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic intuition is that getting an arithmetic problem right requires getting several things right together. Imagine that the probability of predicting each digit correctly improves smoothly as the model gets better. If we score the whole answer as correct only when every digit is correct, then, under a simple independence assumption, the probability of success is that per-digit probability raised to the number of digits.

That can make gradual improvements look quite abrupt. When per-digit accuracy is low, the chance of getting the entire answer right is tiny. Once per-digit accuracy is sufficiently high, whole-answer accuracy rises rapidly, and eventually it saturates. So you can see an S-shaped curve without assuming that the model suddenly acquired a fundamentally new capability.

The point is that the shape of the curve alone doesn’t establish a discontinuity in learning. It can come from how smaller improvements combine and how we measure success.

r001.rationale: The response explains that whole-answer success requires every digit to be correct and models that probability as per-digit accuracy raised to the number of digits, producing a steep, S-shaped rise as per-digit accuracy improves.
